stem: A confused older adult repeatedly tries to climb over full-length bed rails. Which safety concern should the nurse recognize?

options.A: Keep full-length rails raised and increase rounding because rails remain appropriate fall-prevention barriers even when the client is climbing over them.
options.B: Pad the rail openings and continue full-length rails without reassessment because padding alone removes the main entrapment and climbing risks.
options.C: Use all full-length rails whenever confusion worsens because additional rails reduce unsupervised bed exit without creating meaningful additional hazards.
options.D: Full-length rails can create entrapment and climbing-related fall hazards, so the nurse should reassess whether the rails increase rather than reduce this client's risk.

rationale: FDA bed-safety guidance identifies frail, elderly and confused patients as vulnerable to bed-rail entrapment and notes that climbing over rails can result in more serious falls. FDA recommends individual patient assessment rather than routine bed-rail use. D therefore identifies the relevant safety concern. A and C assume rails are protective despite observed climbing, and B incorrectly assumes padding eliminates the need for reassessment.
educational_objective: Reassess bed-rail use in confused older adults because rails may create entrapment or climbing-related fall hazards rather than reliably preventing injury.
source_document_title: Hospital Beds; A Guide to Bed Safety — Bed Rails in Hospitals, Nursing Homes and Home Health Care

source_locator: FDA Hospital Beds page — patient assessment/entrapment data; 'A Guide to Bed Safety' — Patient Safety and Meeting Patients' Needs for Safety; Recommendations for Health Care Providers Using Adult Portable Bed Rails — individual assessment and climbing risk.
source_claim_supported: Older/confused patients are at increased entrapment risk; bed rails can lead to more serious injuries when patients climb over them; bed-rail use should be based on individualized assessment rather than routine use.

source_original.stem: A confused older adult repeatedly tries to climb over full-length bed rails. Which safety concern should the nurse recognize?

options.A: Keep full-length rails raised and increase rounding, because rails remain appropriate fall-prevention barriers even when the client has begun climbing over them.
options.B: Pad the rail openings and continue full-length rails without reassessment, because padding alone removes the main entrapment and climbing risks.
options.C: Use all full-length rails whenever confusion worsens, because additional rails reduce unsupervised bed exit without creating meaningful additional hazards.
options.D: Full-length rails can create entrapment or climbing hazards, so the nurse should assess whether the rails increase rather than reduce this client's risk.

source_original.rationale: FDA warns that bed rails can create entrapment hazards, particularly for older or confused patients, and recommends individualized assessment. Option D recognizes that the rail itself may increase this client's risk. Option A assumes a rail remains protective despite observed climbing. Option B assumes padding alone removes the need to reassess the rail. Option C incorrectly assumes that adding more rails cannot introduce additional hazards.
source_original.source_detail: FDA Hospital Beds and Bed-Rail Safety — Bed-rail entrapment/fall hazards and patient assessment: frail, elderly, confused patients are vulnerable; rails require individualized risk-benefit assessment rather than automatic use. Current FDA hospital-bed and bed-rail safety guidance; rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: asepsis, equipment/environmental safety, incident/event prevention and infection-control activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained key and construct; made the climbing-related fall hazard explicit because FDA directly identifies more serious injury from falls when patients climb over rails, and tied the response to individualized reassessment rather than automatic rail continuation.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Bed-rail entrapment and climbing-related fall risk
audit_findings.currentness: Current FDA bed-safety resources live in 2026.
audit_findings.exact_locator: Hospital Beds page plus FDA Bed Safety Guide and health-care-provider rail recommendations.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Entrapment, high-risk confusion/age, climbing-related fall injury and individual assessment are directly FDA-supported.

distractor_audit.B: Padding does not replace patient reassessment.
distractor_audit.C: Routine additional rails contradict individualized assessment and can add hazards.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D addresses both entrapment and climbing hazards using individualized assessment.
audit_findings.cueing: All options concern rail-management decisions; no second answer.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Verified bed rails are not portrayed as universally harmful; final wording is individualized to this climbing/confused client.
